title: Vocabulary, Synonyms, and Controlled Labels
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Vocabulary, Synonyms, and Controlled Labels. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Labels name choices, categories, actions, and states. Good labels use language people recognise, distinguish neighbouring concepts, and remain stable enough to support learning. Controlled vocabulary gives a system consistent preferred terms while preserving synonyms, aliases, and search cues for the language people actually use.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not label from an internal organisation chart. Study customer language, search queries, support conversations, and task context. Test labels in the place where they will be used: a heading can be clear in isolation but misleading beside competing options.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at govern the bridge between vocabularies?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Products serve several vocabularies at once: the words people use, terms required by a domain, labels embedded in systems, and language used by search or analytics. A controlled vocabulary does not force everyone to use one phrase. It defines preferred concepts, accepted synonyms, disambiguation, scope, and ownership so different language can resolve to consistent meaning.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Candidate language comes from interviews, query logs, call transcripts, letters, analytics, and specialist review. The team tests labels in context through first-click, tree, and comprehension tasks. A term is not adopted “clear” because participants recognise it; they must predict the destination or consequence accurately. Confident misinterpretation is a rejection signal.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Vocabulary changes are versioned because they affect search mappings, content, components, training, support scripts, analytics, and sometimes legal meaning. The output includes synonym redirects and a migration plan. lesson 131 then uses these governed labels to establish wayfinding through the complex space.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: security settings?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Two-step verification,” “two-factor authentication,” “2FA,” and “login codes” may refer to related concepts. A vocabulary system can recognise the variants while distinguishing authentication method, recovery code, trusted device, and account recovery—preventing a friendly label from collapsing important security differences.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a vocabulary bridge?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Collect terms from user research, search logs, support, domain experts, policy, analytics, and existing content. Identify preferred labels, synonyms, abbreviations, homonyms, broader and narrower terms, and context. Controlled vocabulary creates consistent indexing and display while preserving the language people actually use for retrieval.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define every preferred term, scope, examples, exclusions, owner, and relationships. Use audience-facing labels where clarity permits; retain authoritative terms when they carry legal or technical meaning, then explain them. Map synonyms in search instead of forcing users to guess the official word.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test sibling distinctness, destination prediction, scanning, translation, and assistive-technology pronunciation. Monitor zero results, reformulation, support language, and inconsistent authoring. A vocabulary changes with products and communities, so provide contribution, review, version, and deprecation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not pursue uniformity at the expense of meaning. Different audiences may legitimately use different labels; the system should map them to shared concepts without pretending language is neutral.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build a concept record that survives channels
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a concept record that survives channels?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Terms are tested in sentences and decisions, not as isolated preferences. Participants predict destinations, explain state, and choose an action. Staff and subject experts verify domain accuracy. Search logs and support language reveal new variants.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confident wrong interpretation is more consequential than a term that takes a moment to learn, because it can produce the wrong action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Change requires impact analysis. Renaming a state affects event data, component APIs, historical analytics, notifications, help, localisation, and staff language. The team records whether the concept changed or only its label, supports aliases and migration, and preserves historical meaning. Vocabulary governance is semantic versioning for the experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: identity security?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Two-factor authentication, verification code, trusted device, recovery code, and account recovery are related but not synonyms. A controlled vocabulary can accept everyday queries while preventing an article or support agent from recommending the wrong security path.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Every renamed label creates a migration problem for existing users, documentation, analytics, and support. Treat terminology as product infrastructure, not decorative copy.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Treat vocabulary as a managed system. Define preferred terms, synonyms, deprecated labels, scope notes, translations, and ownership. Align labels across navigation, headings, search, metadata, analytics, support, and staff guidance so a person is not required to learn a new word at every touchpoint.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use evidence from queries and support language to expose gaps between organisational and customer vocabulary.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Internal-term default: operational jargon becomes the primary label for a customer task. Synonym blindness: search and support fail because only one term is recognised. Uncontrolled rename: a new label breaks learned behaviour, analytics, and documentation. Ambiguous sibling: nearby labels overlap, so people cannot predict the difference.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A customer searches “refund,” but the help centre calls it “post-purchase adjustment.” The organisation has a precise internal term; the customer has a real question. Findability fails at the label.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 129 selected the organisation scheme. Labels make that scheme legible. lesson 131 applies both to navigation and orientation through a complex system.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find three labels in a product that require insider knowledge. For each, write the customer’s likely term and the evidence you would need before renaming it.
